idiom_name: visitor interfaces with default implementations + is capability checks (sealed + when when the set is closed)
implementation_notes: Kotlin carries both halves in a lighter form than Java: an interface member may have a body, so the visitor's default behaviour lives on the base interface and an extended visitor is a second interface that inherits it (`interface UnionVisitor : Visitor { fun visitUnion(u: UnionShape) }`), while the element negotiates with a plain `is` check and falls back to the default. Extending an existing operation reuses code either by class inheritance (`class UnionArea : Area(), UnionVisitor`) or by interface delegation (`class UnionArea(private val base: Area) : Visitor by base, UnionVisitor`), which is Kotlin's substitute for inheriting a visitor's recursion. Kotlin's own answer to the underlying expression problem is a sealed hierarchy plus an exhaustive `when`: sealed subtypes are fixed at compile time in the same module and the compiler proves coverage, so the visitor is only justified for hierarchies that must stay open to other modules.
pitfalls: Interface members with bodies make a forgotten case in visitDefault a silent no-op - throw there unless a no-op is correct for every future element kind.
`is`-based negotiation is a runtime test: when the extended interface is absent the default path runs, so a missing handler surfaces as default behaviour instead of a compile error.
Sealed hierarchies are the alternative, not a variant: subtypes must be declared in the same module and package, so `when` exhaustiveness can never cover element kinds added later by another module.
Interface delegation inherits only the members the delegate's type declares: a member added later to the delegated interface must be implemented explicitly or the delegation stops compiling.
